title: AI Safety (CS 2881) Lecture 7: Lab vs Field: Guest lecture by Joel Becker
summary: METR researcher reconciles fast-rising benchmark time horizons with the 2025 RCT slowdown and thin labor-market effects, attributing the gap to context, messiness, scoring and reliability.

assertions.quote: And in fact, we we observe that they go slower.

verdicts.note: Accurately reports METR's July 2025 RCT (16 devs, ~19% slower); the finding is specific to that setting and early-2025 tools.

assertions.quote: retradicting how much they were sped up in the past on the issues in this study predict that they went 20% faster

verdicts.note: METR found devs believed they were ~20% faster while measured slower; other studies also show self-reports outrunning measured gains.

assertions.quote: if you plot that over calendar time you see something that kind of looks exponential.

verdicts.note: METR's 2025 time-horizon study found ~7-month doubling (faster in 2024-25); later measurements stayed on or above trend, with wide error bars.

assertions.quote: The 80% time horizons are much lower. They're something like a factor of five lower, I think.

verdicts.note: METR's own analysis: 80%-success horizons are roughly 4-5x shorter than 50% horizons.

assertions.quote: benchmarks look very bullish. This RCT looks much less bullish.

verdicts.note: METR's own analysis and follow-ups found many benchmark-passing patches aren't mergeable; messy, high-context work lags benchmark scores.

assertions.quote: you both need to verify whether they're right or wrong, and then if they're wrong, you need to redo the work.

verdicts.note: A reasonable explanation consistent with METR's 44% acceptance and review overhead; the specific threshold is conjecture.

assertions.quote: AIS do do worse in sort of larger environments by lines of code or numbers of files

verdicts.note: Consistent across Stanford's data, METR's mature-repo slowdown and long-context degradation results.

assertions.quote: It seems totally plausible to me that by the channel that you're pointing at um junior developers will be will be sped up more.

verdicts.note: Field experiments (Microsoft/Accenture RCTs, Brynjolfsson) found the largest gains for less-experienced or less-familiar workers and routine tasks; METR found slowdowns for deep-familiarity experts.

assertions.quote: to the extent that we're seeing economic impacts so far it's just for these um uh very young people in very AI exposed industries

verdicts.note: Stanford 'Canaries' (2025) found ~13% relative employment decline for 22-25-year-olds in AI-exposed jobs, but rates, over-hiring correction and other macro factors also matter.

assertions.quote: outcome measures that um uh that I that I don't have a huge amount of faith in things like you know lines of code

verdicts.note: Stanford and GitClear both found increased short-term churn/rework with AI, so raw commit/PR counts inflate apparent gains.

assertions.quote: AI tooling companies are producing benefits for the developer experience more than more than productivity benefits at recent margins

verdicts.note: Consistent with METR's perception gap and surveys reporting less frustration/fatigue; a plausible explanation rather than a measured mechanism.
